position_name: Intellectual Property Lawyer — AI-Generated Coursework Ownership and Copyright Liability
representative_actor: IP attorneys, copyright counselors, university legal departments, technology law firms (e.g., Baker McKenzie, Greenberg Traurig), Vietnam IP Office, US Copyright Office
central_claim: The question of who owns AI-generated student coursework and whether its submission constitutes fraud depends critically on copyright law, AI service terms, and attribution—not on detection technology. Universities accepting undetected AI-generated work assume copyright liability and may be implicitly licensing third-party training data without consent.
key_evidence_they_would_cite: US Copyright Office 2023 policy (human authorship required for copyright protection); OpenAI TOS assigning output ownership to users; Vietnam IP Law 2022 amendments (effective 2026) requiring 'significant creative contribution' for copyright; EU AI Act Articles 53(1)(c-d) on training data compliance; Copyright Directive exceptions for text-and-data mining; Zarya of the Dawn case (Midjourney images non-copyrightable); federal court decisions denying copyright to purely AI-generated works; Stanford study on disparate detection impact on ESL writers (establishing detection unreliability).
policy_preference: Universities must clarify: (1) whether student submission of AI output constitutes implied warranty of authorship (breach of contract/misrepresentation); (2) whether universities claiming copyright over student work for detection database purposes own the underlying work; (3) whether accepting undetected AI text exposes universities to DMCA liability if that text contains training-data copyright infringement; (4) Vietnamese law requirement for 'significant human creative contribution'—what constitutes sufficient contribution in academic context; (5) OpenAI indemnity clauses for educational users; (6) whether honor codes stating 'work is my own' create estoppel against later detection; (7) Title VI compliance for using biased detection tools as proof of misconduct.
what_they_reject: Rejecting: (1) the assumption that 'AI detection = proof of fraud' without legal due process; (2) the use of detection tools as sole basis for discipline without addressing their disparate impact on ESL students; (3) policies that assume universities own student work for any purpose without explicit consent; (4) the notion that copyright law is irrelevant to academic integrity—it defines the very concepts of authorship and ownership; (5) treating AI-generated text submission as inherently fraudulent without analyzing whether the student made 'significant creative contribution' (Vietnam law standard); (6) the idea that OpenAI's output ownership disclaimer eliminates liability for universities accepting such work.
strongest_version_of_argument: Under existing copyright law, AI-generated text cannot receive copyright protection unless the user made substantial creative choices (selection, arrangement, editing, direction). If a student merely inputs a prompt without significant modification of output, the submission may have no copyright at all—making it unclear what the student 'owns' to submit. OpenAI contractually assigns output ownership to users, but that doesn't resolve whether the student can legally use it in an academic context that requires original work. If universities detect but do NOT discipline the violation, they have implicitly accepted and licensed the work, potentially exposing themselves to liability if that work contains training-data infringement. If universities DO discipline based on detection alone, they face Title VI disparate impact litigation because detection tools flag ESL writers at 10+ percentage points higher rates. The strongest legal position: universities should NOT rely on detection tools as evidence; instead, they should require students to submit process documentation (drafts, prompts, edits) that demonstrates creative contribution. This shifts burden to students to prove originality while protecting universities from both detection tool bias and copyright liability. Vietnamese law 2026 amendments explicitly require assessment of human creative contribution—universities can operationalize this through process documentation rather than detection algorithms.
what_the_debate_missed_by_excluding_this: The debate conflated 'detection' with 'due process' without examining the legal liability universities face. Three critical points were missed: (1) Detection tools are not admissible evidence in legal proceedings due to known bias against ESL writers—using them as sole basis for discipline creates Title VI liability; (2) Copyright law, not honor codes, determines whether submitting AI-generated work is fraud. If a student made 'significant creative contribution' (Vietnam 2022 law), the submission may be entirely legal. The debate assumed 'AI use = dishonesty' without legal analysis of what constitutes authorship under copyright law; (3) Universities accepting undetected AI-generated work assume copyright liability if that work was trained on copyrighted material and inadvertently reproduces it. The debate focused on student discipline but not on institutional risk management.
response_to_left_wing: The left-wing position correctly identifies structural injustice but misses the legal dimension: detection tools ARE a civil rights issue, but not primarily because they penalize students—because they expose universities to Title VI liability when used for high-stakes discipline. The structural fix is not 'abolish detection' but 'require process documentation instead of algorithms.' This protects both student rights AND protects universities from litigation. Lawyers fully support the left-wing call for assessment redesign, but for a legal reason: process portfolios (drafts, prompts, edits) are admissible evidence of originality, while AI detection scores are not. The difference: detection flags a suspicious output; process documentation proves a student's creative contribution or fails to do so. Left-wing educators and lawyers converge on assessment redesign as the legally sound alternative.
response_to_right_wing: The right-wing position on individual responsibility is undermined by copyright law: if universities don't clarify AI output ownership and copyright status, individual students cannot possibly know their rights and duties. The right-wing preference for market-based credentialing (employers verify competency) is compatible with legal due process—but only if universities stop using biased detection tools and start documenting which skills students actually developed. A student disciplined for undetected AI use has a legal claim that they were not on notice of the university's AI policy; a student disciplined via detection algorithm has a Title VI claim of disparate impact. The legal position aligns with the right-wing's call for clearer rules and reduced government regulation—the fix is to specify in student contracts exactly what constitutes AI usage and what process evidence is required.
response_to_economist: The economist's cost-benefit analysis of spot vivas (15% sampling, 10 hours per 300-student cycle) is legally compatible but incomplete: oral exams prove student learning without the disparate-impact liability of detection tools, AND they reduce institutional risk. From a liability perspective, the cost of a Title VI discrimination lawsuit from ESL students falsely flagged by detection tools far exceeds the 10 hours of faculty time for vivas. The economist should factor in legal costs, not just instructional costs. Universities can optimize: use detection tools as preliminary screening (not as evidence), then use process documentation and spot vivas as admissible proof. This satisfies both cost minimization AND legal due process.
response_to_educator: The educator's call for assessment redesign aligns perfectly with legal obligations: process portfolios and oral exams generate admissible evidence of learning. The educator correctly saw that 'detection tools are not detection of learning,' and the lawyer adds: 'detection tools are not legal evidence.' Both converge: assessment should measure what a student can DO (oral defense, live problem-solving), not what algorithms suspect. Vietnamese law 2026 amendments support this: universities must assess the student's creative contribution to AI-assisted work. The educator and lawyer together provide the institutional blueprint: eliminate detection, shift to process documentation and performance-based assessment.
response_to_technologist: The technologist's critique that 'detection tools don't work and will be collectively defeated' is empirically supported (Liang et al. 2023: 61% false positive rate on ESL essays). The lawyer adds a second reason NOT to rely on detection: even if tools worked perfectly, using them as evidence creates legal liability. A perfect detection algorithm is still a tool that disproportionately impacts ESL writers, potentially violating Title VI. The technologist and lawyer converge on the practical conclusion: stop investing in detection arms races. Instead, invest in process-verification tools that let students demonstrate creative contribution through draft submission, prompt logging, and output editing.
response_to_center: The center's AIAS framework (assessment, infrastructure, support, sanction) is legally sound but needs sharpening: the 'sanction' layer should NOT rely on detection tools due to Title VI liability. The center's pragmatic synthesis must include a legal layer: due process requires that any discipline be based on admissible evidence (process documentation, oral exams) not on algorithmic suspicion. The center's call for 'honor code culture' is legally important because honor codes shift burden to students to assert compliance, establishing intent to rely on university rules. This creates estoppel: a student disciplined for undetected AI use can claim lack of notice; a student who signed an honor code agreeing to original work cannot make that claim. The center should frame honor codes as legal notices, not just cultural values.
claims_they_would_contest: That AI-generated text submitted to university is 'the student's work' unless the student made significant creative contribution as defined by Vietnam IP Law 2022 and US Copyright Office standards.
That detection tools are admissible evidence of academic dishonesty in any legal proceeding (they would be excluded as unreliable and having disparate impact).
That universities own student-submitted work for purposes of building detection databases without explicit consent (copyright assignment requires written agreement).
That OpenAI's assignment of output ownership to users resolves all liability questions (it does not address whether the user can legally use that output in educational contexts).

That high false-positive rates in detection tools can be fixed through better algorithmic training (the problem is structural: non-native English writing patterns are not identical to AI patterns, violating the tool's assumption).
That honor codes create an implied waiver of due process protections (they do not; a student can still challenge discipline based on unreliable evidence).
That universities can unilaterally define 'original work' without reference to copyright law (copyright law defines authorship; universities must align policies with legal standards).
how_including_this_voice_changes_conclus: The legal perspective reframes the entire debate from 'How do we catch AI fraud?' to 'How do we prove student learning while avoiding litigation risk?' This changes three conclusions: (1) Detection tools should NOT be used as primary evidence due to Title VI liability and unreliability—process documentation and performance exams are superior legally and pedagogically; (2) Universities must update policies to align with Vietnam IP Law 2022 (requiring assessment of 'significant creative contribution') and US Copyright Office 2023 guidance (copyright requires human authorship with creative direction); (3) The academic integrity crisis is not primarily a detection problem but a due process problem—students lack clear notice of what constitutes permitted vs. prohibited AI use, and universities lack admissible evidence procedures. Fixing due process (clear policies + process documentation + performance exams) simultaneously addresses learning, fairness, and legal risk.
irreconcilable_disagreements: Between the IP lawyer and detection-tool vendors over evidentiary standards: vendors claim their tools detect AI use; lawyers require proof that detection is accurate enough to meet burden of proof in disciplinary hearings (preponderance of evidence) and that the tool does not have disparate impact. This disagreement is not ideological but technical and legal—vendors have not published evidence meeting these standards. Between copyright owners and universities over training data: OpenAI claims educational use of AI is not infringement; copyright owners argue that student use of ChatGPT to generate coursework may inadvertently reproduce copyrighted material. Universities cannot resolve this disagreement; it requires legislator or court action. Between universities and students over notice: universities claim AI policies are sufficiently clear; students claim policies do not explain what constitutes 'significant creative contribution' under Vietnam law, making compliance impossible. This is an irreconcilable gap until legislatures provide definitions.
real_world_evidence_of_this_position: US Copyright Office 2023 registration guidance (human authorship required); federal court refusal to register Zarya of the Dawn images (Midjourney images not copyrightable); Stanford study (Liang et al. 2023) finding 61% false positive rate on ESL essays; Center for Democracy and Technology brief on Title VI implications of detection tool bias; multiple universities updating AI policies to require process documentation instead of relying on detection (UC Davis, MIT); law review articles (USC IP & Tech Law Society, Syracuse Law Review, Harvard JSEL) examining liability of using biased detection tools; Vietnam IP Office circulars interpreting the 2022 amendments; OpenAI Help Center statement that copyright is assigned to users but doesn't resolve educational-context legality; ProctorU/ExamSoft settling discrimination lawsuits (establishing that algorithmic evidence of dishonesty has legal vulnerabilities).

vietnamese_context_relevance: Vietnam's IP Law 2022 amendments (effective April 1, 2026) explicitly require that AI-generated works receive copyright protection ONLY if the human creator made 'significant creative contribution' in selection, arrangement, or editing. This is stricter than US law (which requires human authorship) and stricter than OpenAI's terms (which assign ownership to the user regardless of creative input). Vietnamese universities can operationalize this standard by requiring process documentation: drafts, prompts, editing logs. If a student submitted only a final product with no documentation of creative direction, Vietnamese law presumes the student did NOT make sufficient creative contribution, shifting burden to the student to prove otherwise. This provides a legal basis for assessment redesign that aligns with Vietnamese law and protects universities from liability. Additionally, Vietnam's national medical licensing exam (starting 2027) and bar exam are high-stakes professional certification contexts where proctoring and process documentation are professionally justified and legally defensible under proportionality principles.
weaknesses_of_this_position: IP lawyers focus on risk management for institutions rather than supporting student learning—framing the issue purely through liability can seem to deprioritize pedagogy (though assessment redesign ultimately serves both).

The legal position requires universities to invest in new assessment infrastructure (process documentation platforms, oral exam scheduling) which may be more costly than maintaining detection tools in the short term (though long-term liability costs favor investment).

Copyright law is unsettled in Vietnam (2022 amendments are new) and internationally (US, EU, and Vietnam have conflicting standards)—lawyers cannot provide definitive guidance until courts rule; this creates uncertainty for universities trying to update policies now.
The IP lawyer's position may be seen as pro-regulation (favoring court enforcement of copyright/Title VI) by those who prefer market-based or honor-code approaches.

Not all students have equal capacity to generate process documentation (e.g., students from countries with restricted internet may not have drafting tools); this requirement could create new equity issues.
The argument assumes copyright law is relevant to academic integrity—some argue academic integrity is a separate ethical domain not reducible to copyright law.
what_would_change_their_mind: Legislation in Vietnam, US, or EU explicitly resolving copyright ownership of AI-generated works and clarifying university responsibilities (removing legal ambiguity).
Published peer-reviewed study showing that detection tools have zero disparate impact and their false positive rate is below 1% on all demographic groups (eliminating Title VI liability concern).
Court decision establishing that universities have qualified immunity from liability for discipline based on detection tools even if tools are biased (removing legal risk deterrent).
Successful student civil rights lawsuit against a university for discrimination based on detection tool bias, establishing precedent that forces policy change (confirming worst-case legal scenario).
OpenAI or other AI vendors publishing indemnification clauses specifically covering educational institutions that use AI-generated text in coursework (transferring liability risk).
Evidence that honor codes alone (without process documentation) reduce AI-assisted dishonesty below X% threshold, suggesting detection is unnecessary (changing cost-benefit calculus).
Arbitration or mediation cases showing that detection tools ARE accepted as admissible evidence in disciplinary proceedings when coupled with student testimony (contradicting legal skepticism).
